Reviving Thorup’s Shortcut Conjecture

**Abstract**

We aim to revive Thorup’s conjecture [Tho92] on the existence of _reachability shortcuts_ with ideal size-diameter tradeoffs. Thorup originally asked whether, given any graph _G_=(_V,E_) with _m_ edges, we can add _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> “shortcut” edges _E_<sub>+</sub> from the transitive closure _E_<sup>∗</sup> of _G_ so that \(dist_{G_+}(u,v)\le m^{o(1)}\) for all \((u,v)\in E^*\), where \(G_+=(V,E\cup E_+)\). The conjecture was refuted by Hesse [Hes03], followed by significant efforts in the last few years to optimize the lower bounds [HP21, LVWX22, BH23a, VXX24, HXX25].

In this paper, we observe that although Hesse refuted the _letter_ of Thorup’s conjecture, his work [Hes03]--and all followup work [HP21, LVWX22, BH23a, VXX24, HXX25]--does not refute the _spirit_ of the conjecture, which should allow _G_<sub>+</sub> to contain both new shortcut edges and _new Steiner vertices_. Our results are as follows.

\(\bullet\) On the positive side, we present explicit attacks that break all known shortcut lower bounds [Hes03, HP21, LVWX22, BH23a, VXX24, HXX25] when Steiner vertices are allowed.

\(\bullet\) On the negative side, we rule out ideal _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>-size, _m_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>-diameter shortcuts whose “thickness” is _t=o_(log_n/_loglog_n_), meaning no path can contain _t_ consecutive Steiner vertices.

\(\bullet\) We propose a candidate hard instance as the next step toward resolving the revised version of Thorup’s conjecture.

Finally, we show promising implications. Almost-optimal parallel algorithms for computing a generalization of the shortcut that _approximately_ preserves distances or flows imply almost- optimal parallel algorithms with _m_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> depth for _exact_ shortcut paths and _exact_ maximum flow. The state-of-the-art algorithms have much worse depth of _n_<sup>1/2+_o_(1)</sup> [RHM<sup>+</sup>23a] and _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> [CKL<sup>+</sup>22], respectively.

## 1 Introduction

One of the grand challenges in parallel computing is to overcome the _transitive closure bottleneck_ \[KK93\]: the observation that computing reachability in directed graphs apparently requires <u>either</u> superlinear work (iterated matrix squaring) to achieve polylog(_n_) depth, or \(n^{\Omega(1)}\) depth to achieve near-linear work. The problem of simultaneously achieving _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> work and _m_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> depth has remained an elusive goal for decades, for reachability and harder problems such as shortest paths and (min-cost) flows.

Naturally, researchers have tried to overcome this bottleneck in various ways. These efforts have been extremely fruitful, leading to the development of _hopsets_ \[Coh00\] for computing approximate shortest paths, _shortcuts_ \[UY91\] to achieve work-depth tradeoffs, min-sketches for estimating transitive closure size \[Coh97\], and attention to graph classes where the bottleneck does not exist, e.g., planar graphs \[KK93\]. In 1992, Thorup \[Tho92\] made a bold, purely combinatorial conjecture that was motivated by the transitive closure bottleneck.

**Conjecture 1** (Thorup’s Shortcut Conjecture \[Tho92\])**.** _Let G_<sup>∗</sup>=(_V,E_<sup>∗</sup>) _be the transitive closure of an arbitrary directed graph G_=(_V,E), with m_=|_E|. There exists a_ shortcut \(E_+\subset E^*\) _with_ \(|E_+|\le m\) _such that_ \(G_+=(V,E\cup E_+)\) _has_ polylog(_n_) _diameter, that is,_ dist<sub>_G_<sub>+</sub></sub>(_u,v_)=polylog(_n), for every_ \((u,v)\in E^*\).

In other words, once the shortcut _E_<sub>+</sub> is discovered in preprocessing, single-source reachability could be computed near-optimally, in \(\tilde{O}(m)\) work and \(\tilde{O}(1)\) depth. Conjecture 1 was known for rooted trees \[Cha87\] with a diameter<sup>1</sup> of \(O(\alpha(n,n))\) and later confirmed for planar graphs \[Tho95\] with a diameter of \(O(\alpha(n,n)log^2n)\).<sup>2</sup> Thorup \[Tho92\] insisted on \(|E_+|\le m\), but one could set any number of thresholds for the shortcut size, e.g., _O(m),m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>_,n_<sup>1.5</sup>_,n_<sup>1.99</sup>, etc. In 2003 Hesse \[Hes03\] refuted Conjecture 1 and many weaker versions of it.

**Theorem 1.1** (Hesse \[Hes03\])**.** _For any_ \(\epsilon>0\) _and n sufficiently large, there exist n-vertex graphs G_=(_V,E_) _and_ \(G'=(V,E')\) _with_ \(m,m'\) _edges, respectively, such that:_

• \(m=\Theta(n^{19/17})\) _and any shortcut for G with o(n_<sup>1/17</sup>) _diameter must have_ \(\Omega(mn^{1/17})\) _edges._<tbc>

• \(m'=n^{1+\epsilon}\) _and any shortcut for_ \(G'\) _with n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> _diameter must have_ \(\Omega(n^{2-\epsilon})\) _edges._

Theorem 1.1 precludes the most optimistic outcome, but it still leaves open many fascinating and potentially practical questions, such as: what diameter can be achieved with \(\tilde{O}(m)\)- or \(\tilde{O}(n)\)- size shortcuts? And can such shortcuts be computed efficiently? It is now known that the optimum diameters for \(\tilde{O}(n)\)- and \(\tilde{O}(m)\)-size shortcuts are in the ranges \([\tilde{\Omega}(n^{1/4}),\tilde{O}(n^{1/3})]\), and \([\tilde{\Omega}(n^{2/9}),\tilde{O}(n^{2/3}/m^{1/3})]\), respectively, and that the upper bounds can be attained in polynomial time. See  1 for details and references.

### 1.1 Reviving Conjecture 1

The shortcut problem, as Thorup \[Tho92\] originally defined it, is now well on its way to being completely solved, as we have narrowed down the correct exponent to a small range and just a couple plausible answers: 1/4 or 1/3.

However, Conjecture 1 is perhaps _too strict_ from the algorithmic perspective. This is because the final goal is to somehow replace a directed graph _G_=(_V,E_) with _any G_<sub>+</sub> of comparable size such that (1) the transitive closure of _G_ can be extracted from the transitive closure of _G_<sub>+</sub>, and (2) every \((u,v)\in E^*\) is witnessed by a "short" _u-v_ path in _G_<sub>+</sub>. We propose the following small fix to Conjecture 1 by allowing _G_<sub>+</sub> to introduce _Steiner vertices_.

<sup>1</sup>The _diameter_ of a directed graph is defined to be the largest _finite_ distance. <sup>2</sup>A corollary of Thorup’s planar reachability oracle \[Tho04\] implies a shortcut with size _O(n_log_n_) and diameter 4.

**Conjecture 2** (Steiner Shortcut Conjecture)**.** _Let G_<sup>∗</sup>=(_V,E_<sup>∗</sup>) _be the transitive closure of a directed graph G_=(_V,E). There exists a graph_ \(G_+=(V\cup V_+,E\cup E_+)\) _such that_

• _G_<sub>+</sub> _captures the transitive closure of G, i.e., for all_ \((u,v)\in V\times V\)_, v is reachable from u in G iff it is reachable from u in G_<sub>+</sub>.<tbc>

• \(|E_+|=\widetilde{O}(|E|)\);<tbc>

• _G_<sub>+</sub> _has_ polylog(_n_) _diameter, i.e.,_ \(\forall(u,v)\in E^*\), dist<sub>_G_<sub>+</sub></sub>(_u,v_)=polog(_n_).

We are not the first to propose the use of Steiner points. Berman, Bhattacharyya, Grigorescu, Raskhodnikova, Woodruff, and Yaroslavtsev \[BBG<sup>+</sup>14\] proved that if _G_ is a DAG with dimension _d_, meaning there is a reachability-preserving embedding into the oriented hypergrid \[_n_\]_<sup>d</sup>_, then it has a diameter-2 graph _G_<sub>+</sub> with _O(n_log_<sup>d</sup>n_) shortcuts. However, the prior work on Steiner shortcuts \[BBG<sup>+</sup>14, Ras10\] has no bearing on Conjecture 2.

## 1.2 Contributions

The purpose of this paper is to explore Conjecture 2 and the power of Steiner vertices more generally in constructing shortcuts. We are _uncertain_ about the truth of Conjecture 2 and our goal is to raise it as an open problem. Although Conjecture 2 can be refuted using known techniques when the size of the Steiner shortcut is limited to \(|E_+|\le|E|^{1-\epsilon}\) for a constant \(\epsilon\) (see Section A), once we permit \(|E_+|=\widetilde{O}(|E|)\), all known techniques become ineffective.

Indeed, our main contribution is to carefully demonstrate why the lower bounds of Hesse \[Hes03\], Huang and Pettie \[HP21\], Lu, Williams, Wein, and Xu \[LVWX22\], Williams, Xu, and Xu \[VXX24\], and Hoppenworth, Xu, and Xu \[HXX25\] fail catastrophically when Steiner vertices are allowed. These results are presented in Section 2.

Our second result, presented in Section 3, can be viewed as either partially refuting Conjecture 2 or identifying the crucial property that the shortcut for Conjecture 2 must satisfy. Specifically, we show that the shortcut must have a sufficiently large _thickness_, defined as follows.

**Definition 1.2** (Thickness)**.** Let \(G_+=(V\cup V_+,E\cup E_+)\) be a Steiner shortcut graph for _G_=(_V,E_). We say _G_<sub>+</sub> has _thickness t_ (or is _t-thick_) if every path in _G_<sub>+</sub> has at most _t_-1 consecutive Steiner vertices from _V_<sub>+</sub>.

For example, if \(V_+=\emptyset\) (there are no Steiner vertices) then the thickness is 1, and all prior lower bounds \[Hes03, HP21, LVWX22, VXX24, HXX25\] are merely for 1-thick shortcut graphs. A 2-thick shortcut graph is one for which the in- and out-neighbors of _V_<sub>+</sub>-vertices are all original _V_ -vertices.

It turns out that almost all existing lower bounds - including the state of the art from \[VXX24, HXX25\] - break once we allow Steiner shortcuts of thickness two. Our main result in Section 3 is to show that thickness two is nonetheless insufficient for general graphs:

**Theorem 1.3.** _For_ \(t\ge 1\)_, there exists an m-edge graph G such that every t-thick Steiner shortcut graph G_<sub>+</sub> _for G either has diameter_ \(m^{\Omega(1/t)}\) _or_ \(m^{1+\Omega(1/t)}\) _edges._

In other words, Theorem 1.3 refutes Conjecture 2 for any fixed _t_, and in fact the proof goes through for any _t=o_(log_n/_loglog_n_). This implies that any upper bound for Conjecture 2 would require a somewhat intricate connection between the Steiner vertices.

Roughly speaking, the "hard" graphs used to prove Theorem 1.3 are a family G_<sub>k</sub>_, which are constructed as the _k_-fold product of a base graph, where _k\>t_. This graph class is _highly structured_, which actually makes it too easy to shortcut with Steiner vertices; in particular, the _k_-fold product G_<sub>k</sub>_ can be shortcut with thickness _t=k_+1. A natural and generic way to make this graph class more difficult to shortcut is to discard each edge with some probability _p_ inversely proportional to the diameter; denote this noised class as \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(p)\). It is an open problem whether \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(p)\) suffices to refute Conjecture 2. As mild evidence of the hardness of this graph family, we show that, unlike G_<sub>k</sub>_, it is resistant to _t_-thick Steiner shortcuts for \(t\le 8k/7\). See Section 3 for a more detailed discussion.

## Potential Implications.

If Conjecture 2 turns out to be true, this would have exciting algorithmic applications. Most notably, it would suggest a promising approach for solving parallel directed reachability with near-linear work and polylog depth.

In the directed reachability problem, we are given as input a graph _G_ and a vertex pair _s,t_, and asked to report whether there exists any path from _s_ to _t_. While low-depth algorithms are known if we allow polynomial work, it is still unclear what depth is possible if we restrict ourselves to _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> work. A depth of _n_ is trivial and was the best known for a long time. A breakthrough of Fineman in 2018 achieved depth _n_<sup>2/3</sup> \[Fin20\], which was later improved to _n_<sup>1/2+_o_(1)</sup> \[JLS19\]. The _n_<sup>1/2+_o_(1)</sup> bound can also be generalized to exact shortest paths \[CFR20, RHM<sup>+</sup>23b\].

All known _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>-work algorithms with sublinear depth rely on the following basic approach: **1)** compute a shortcut _E_<sub>+</sub> with diameter _h_ **2)** run BFS from _s_ in \(G_+=(V,E\cup E')\). The existing work has focused on optimizing step 1, and there is still potential for further progress in this direction. But such progress has a hard barrier: even with the perfect hopset construction, the lower bounds of \[HXX25\] proves that this approach could never lead to depth _o(n_<sup>2/9</sup>).

Observe, however, that the framework would work just as well if we replaced \(E'\) with a _Steiner_ shortcut. So if Conjecture 2 turned out to be true, this would suggest a natural approach for overcoming the above barrier and achieving polylog(_n_) depth. An analogous framework is also frequently used in other models of computation (dynamic, distributed, streaming), and in all those cases a Steiner shortcut would work just as well as a regular one.

The main body of the paper focuses exclusively on the simplest case of (Steiner) shortcuts for reachability because even here we are not sure if Conjecture 2 is true or false. But if the conjecture ends up being true, then one can state a natural generalization of the conjecture for shortest paths (a Steiner hopset) and maximum flow (a low-congestion Steiner shortcut): see Section 4 for more details.

## Connection to Circuit Complexity.

While Steiner shortcuts are primarily motivated by the algorithmic applications mentioned above, they are also a natural combinatorial question in their own<tbc>

<tbc>right. Our Conjecture 2 can be recast in terms of circuit complexity. Consider a multi-input, multi- output circuit _C_ consisting solely of unbounded fan-in OR gates. We would like to "compress" _C_ into an equivalent circuit of comparable size but smaller depth. Conjecture 2 is equivalent to Conjecture 3 below; none of the prior work on depth-reduction \[Hås86, Sch82, Sch83, RM97, DRNV16, GKW21\] directly applies to Conjecture 3.

**Conjecture 3.** _Suppose_ \(C:\{0,1\}^a\rightarrow\{0,1\}^b\) _is a circuit consisting solely of OR gates and m wires. There is a logically equivalent circuit_ \(C_+:\{0,1\}^a\rightarrow\{0,1\}^b\) _that has_ \(\widetilde{O}(m)\) _wires and depth_ polylog(_m)._

### Organization.

In Section 2 we give a self-contained exposition of Hesse’s lower bound for (non- Steiner) shortcuts, which we denote by graph family G_<sub>k</sub>_; we will later use this same graph for Theorem 1.3. We then show that the lower bound fails once Steiner vertices are allowed. In Section C we also show how Steiner vertices break the lower bound of \[VXX24\].<sup>3</sup> All other existing lower bounds that we know of can be broken in a similar fashion using Steiner vertices, but we omit the details.

Section 3 contains our thickness lower bounds. We prove Theorem 1.3. We also formalize the noised graph family \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k\)--our candidate hard instance for Conjecture 2--and prove that shortcutting \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k\) requires strictly higher thickness than the one for G_<sub>k</sub>_.

In Section 4 we discuss generalizations of Steiner shortcuts to Steiner hopsets and Steiner low-congestion shortcuts.

## 2 Hesse’s Counterexample Graphs G_<sub>k</sub>_

In this section we review Hesse’s lower bound construction \[Hes03\] and illustrate why his argument breaks down when Steiner vertices are allowed.<sup>4</sup> The attack presented for Hesse’s construction also applies, with suitable modifications, to all subsequent lower bound \[HP21, LVWX22, VXX24, HXX25\]; for details of how to do this with \[VXX24\] in particular, see Appendix C. The reason we describe Hesse’s counterexample in detail is that it is the basis for the lower bounds of Section 3.

Following \[Hes03\] we construct a family of graphs G_<sub>k</sub>_, \(k\ge 2\). Each graph \(G=(V,E)\in\mathcal{G}_k\) will have an associated set of critical vertex pairs \(P\subseteq V\times V\) such that any reachability shortcut of _G_ has size at least |_P_| or hop diameter at least poly(_n_) between some pair of vertices \((s,t)\in P\). The properties of graph family G_<sub>k</sub>_ can be summarized in the following theorem.

**Theorem 2.1** (Cf. \[Hes03, Theorem 4.1\])**.** _Let k\>_1 _be an integer and_ \(\epsilon=\Omega(1/k)\). G_<sub>k</sub> is an infinite family of n-vertex, n_<sup>1+_O_(1_/k_)</sup>_-edge directed graphs. Each graph_ \(G=(V,E)\in\mathcal{G}_k\) _has an associated set of critical vertex pairs_ \(P\subseteq V\times V\) _of size_ \(|P|=\Omega(n^{1.5-\epsilon})\)_. For any shortcut set_ \(E_+\subseteq E^*\) _of G, where G_<sup>∗</sup>=(_V,E_<sup>∗</sup>) _is the transitive closure of G, either_

• \(|E_+|\ge|P|\)_, or_<tbc>

• _There is a pair of vertices_ \((s,t)\in P\) _such that_ \(dist_{G_+}(s,t)=n^{\Omega(1/k)}\) _in_ \(G_+=(V,E\cup E_+)\).

In Section 2.3, we show that Hesse’s construction and argument fails in the presence of Steiner vertices, as captured by the following theorem.

<sup>3</sup>The most recent \(\Omega(n^{2/9})\) lower bound of \[HXX25\] is a slightly optimized version of \[VXX24\] and can be broken in the same way. <sup>4</sup>Technically, we consider a slight variation of Hesse’s construction, decreasing the density of the graph to improve our achievable thickness lower bounds from \(\sqrt{logn}\) to log_n/_loglog_n_. This modification has no significant effect on the analysis in the non-Steiner setting nor for breaking the construction via Steiner points.

**Theorem 2.2.** _Let_ \(k\ge 2\) _be an integer, and let_ \(G=(V,E)\in\mathcal{G}_k\) _be an n-vertex, n_1+_O_(1_/k_)_-edge graph with associated critical vertex pairs_ \(P\subseteq V\times V\)_. Then G admits a k-thick Steiner shortcut graph_ \(G_+=(V\cup V_+,E\cup E_+)\) _with_ \(|E_+|=|E|/n^{\Omega(1/k)}\)_, such that every_ \((s,t)\in P\) _has_ dist_G_+(_s,t_)=_k._ _Remark_ 2.3. All existing lower-bound constructions for (non-Steiner) shortcut sets have the same high-level structure: they tailor the construction to produce a set of critical vertex pairs _P_, and then show that these particular pairs are hard to shortcut. The constructions make no claims about other vertex pairs. For this reason, to show that these lower-bound proofs fail in our new setting, it is enough to show that the critical pairs in particular can be shortcut using Steiner vertices. We strongly believe that for all these constructions one can in fact use Steiner vertices to shortcut _all_ pairs in the graph, but we did not think this would be instructive, since by design only the critical pairs have interesting structure. In Section 3 we show that Theorem 2.2 is essentially tight for the family G_k_, in that any _t_-thick Steiner shortcut set with \(t\checkmark k\) must have size superlinear in _m_ or diameter polynomial in _m_. Before reviewing Hesse’s construction of G_k_ we begin with G1, which introduces some of the key ideas and is sufficient to prove lower bounds on \(\tilde{O}(n)\)-size shortcuts; see Huang and Pettie \[HP21\]. ## 2.1 Warm-up Construction -- Graph Family G1 We construct a graph family G1 that does not quite imply polynomial diameter lower bounds for \(\tilde{O}(m)\)-size shortcut sets. This will motivate some of the design choices introduced in the graph family G_k_ in Section 2.2. Graph family G1 is parameterized by constants \(c\in\mathbb{R}^+\) and \(d\in\mathbb{N}^+\). We denote a specific parameterization of G1 by G1(_c,d_). The size of each graph \(G=(V,E)\in\mathcal{G}_1(c,d)\) is controlled by a parameter \(r\in\mathbb{N}^+\). ### Vertex Set _V_ . Let \(\ell=r^c\). Graph _G_ has \(\ell+1\) layers, \(L_0,L_1,\dots,L_\ell\). The vertices of each layer can be written as a collection of points in a _d_-dimensional grid. Formally, for \(i\in[0,\ell]\), we define _Li_ to be \(L_i=\{i\}\times(-r(r+1)\ell,r(r+1)\ell]^d,\) and let \(V=\cup_{i=0}^\ell L_i\). ### Edge Set _E_ . Let \(B(r,d)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^d\) denote the set of all integer vectors \(\vec{v}\) in Z_d_ of magnitude \(\|\vec{v}\|\le r\), where \(\|\cdot\|\) denotes the standard Euclidean norm. Let \(\mathcal{B}(r,d)\subseteq B(r,d)\) denote the set of extreme points of the convex hull of _B(r,d_). By Bárány and Larman \[BL98\], \(|\mathcal{B}(r,d)|=\Theta\left(r^{d\cdot\frac{d-1}{d+1}}\right)\). The edge set _E_ of _G_ consists of all \((x,y)\in V\times V\) where \(x=(i,p)\in L_i,\)
\(y=(i+1,p+\vec{v})\in L_{i+1},\)
\(\text{and}\vec{v}\in\mathcal{B}(r,d).\) ### Critical Pairs and Critical Paths. We will define a collection of vertex pairs and associated paths in _G_ that are particularly useful in the analysis of _G_. We first specify a set of source nodes \(S\subseteq L_0\) in the first layer of _G_ that will be useful for defining our set of critical vertex pairs. Let _S_ be the set \(S=\{0\}\times(-r^2\ell,r^2\ell]^d.\) For each vertex \(s=(0,p)\in S\) and a vector \(\vec{v}\in\mathcal{B}(r,d)\), let _t_ be the vertex \(t=(\ell,p+\ell\vec{v})\). Note that _t_ is guaranteed to lie in \(L_\ell\) due to \(p\in(-r^2\ell,r^2\ell]^d\) and \(\|\vec{v}\|\le r\). We call (_s,t_) a _critical vertex pair_;

let \(P\subseteq S\times L_\ell\) denote the set of all critical vertex pairs in _G_. Each \((s,t)\in P\) is identified with the _critical path P<sub>s,t</sub>_, defined as follows.

\(P_{s,t}=((0,p),(1,p+\mathaccent\unknown{v}),\dots,(\ell,p+\ell\mathaccent\unknown{v})).\)

Let \(\mathcal{P}=\{P_{s,t}|(s,t)\in P\}\) be the set of critical paths.

We summarize several properties of graph _G_, critical pairs _P_, and critical paths P in the following lemma, which we state without proof.

**Lemma 2.4** (Cf. \[HP21, Lemma 2.2 and 2.6\])**.** _Graph G and paths_ P _have the following properties:_

**Sizes.** \(|V|=\Theta(r^{c+2d+cd})\), \(|E|=\Theta(r^{d\cdot\frac{d-1}{d+1}}\cdot|V|)\)_, and_ \(|P|=|\mathcal{P}|=\Theta(r^{2d+cd+d\cdot\frac{d-1}{d+1}})\).

**Uniqueness.** _Every path_ \(P_{s,t}\in\mathcal{P}\) _is a unique_ (_s,t)-path in G._

**Disjointness.** _Paths in_ P _are pairwise edge-disjoint._

### A remark on the geometry of graph _G_.

Vertex set _V_ and paths P have a very natural geometric interpretation as an arrangement of points and lines in R<sup>_d_+1</sup>. Notice that the vertices of each path \(P_{s,t}\in\mathcal{P}\) lie on a line of the form \(\{x\cdot(1,\mathaccent\unknown{v})+(0,p)|x\in\mathbb{R}\}\) in R<sup>_d_+1</sup> for \(\mathaccent\unknown{v}\in\mathcal{B}(r,d)\) and \((0,p)\in S\). Moreover, because B(_r,d_) consists only of extreme points, each such direction \(\mathaccent\unknown{v}\) _cannot_ be expressed as a convex combination of other vectors in B(_r,d_). This geometric perspective is useful for interpreting the Uniqueness and Disjointness properties of Lemma 2.4.

### Implications and Limitations of G<sub>1</sub>.

Graph class G<sub>1</sub> already gives an interesting lower bound: any _O(n_)-sized shortcut-set of G<sub>1</sub> has diameter at least \(\Omega(\mathrm{poly}(n))\). This follows almost immediately from Lemma 2.4: Since the critical paths are pairwise disjoint, a shortcut edge can only be relevant to a single critical path, so shortcutting every critical pair would require at least |_P_| edges; by the construction of G<sub>1</sub>, we have \(|P|=\Omega(n)\). Unfortunately it is impossible to have \(|P|=\Omega(m)\) in G<sub>1</sub>. In order to force \(|P|\gg m\), Hesse \[Hes03\] defines graph G_<sub>k</sub>_ to be a kind of _k_-fold product of G<sub>1</sub>.

### Optimizing G<sub>1</sub> for Steiner shortcut lower bounds.

Technically, the construction we consider differs slightly from \[Hes03\] and \[HP21\], although the difference is essentially aesthetic for the non-Steiner parts of our discussion. We define \(L_i=\{i\}\times(-r(r+1)\ell,r(r+1)\ell]^d\) as opposed to \(\{i\}\times(-4r\ell,4r\ell]^d\) as in \[Hes03\]. Consequently, we can define _S_, the starting points of our critical paths, as \(\{0\}\times(-r^2\ell,r^2\ell]^d\). _S_ is instead defined as \(\{0\}\times(-2r\ell,2r\ell]^d\) in \[Hes03\]. This means that in Hesse’s construction only a constant fraction of vertices in the starting layer are the first vertex in a critical path; for our modified construction, all but a vanishing fraction of the vertices are. When we prove Theorem 1.3 via Theorem 3.1, this makes the difference between a thickness lower bound of \(o(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}n})\) versus _o_(log_n/_loglog_n_).

## 2.3 Breaking Hesse’s Counterexamples using Steiner Vertices

In this section we will show how Steiner vertices break Hesse’s counterexample argument. We will achieve this by proving Theorem 2.2, restated for convenience.

**Theorem 2.2.** _Let_ \(k\ge 2\) _be an integer, and let_ \(G=(V,E)\in\mathcal{G}_k\) _be an n-vertex, n_<sup>1+_O_(1_/k_)</sup>_-edge graph with associated critical vertex pairs_ \(P\subseteq V\times V\)_. Then G admits a k-thick Steiner shortcut graph_ \(G_+=(V\cup V_+,E\cup E_+)\) _with_ \(|E_+|=|E|/n^{\Omega(1/k)}\)_, such that every_ \((s,t)\in P\) _has_ dist<sub>_G_<sub>+</sub></sub>(_s,t_)=_k._

Let \(G\in\mathcal{G}_k\) be the given graph, parameterized by \(r\in\mathbb{N}^+\). Each critical pair \((s,t)\in P\) is of the form \((((0,0),p),((\ell,0),p+\ell\vec{v}))\), for some _p_=(_p_<sub>0</sub>_,...,p_<sub>_k_-1</sub>) and critical direction \(\vec{v}=(\vec{v}_0,\dots,\vec{v}_{k-1})\). Rather than move from _s_ to _t_ by adding the _k_ critical subdirections in a "round robin" format, we can add each all at once, walking through new Steiner vertices corresponding to points

\(p\rightarrow(p_0+\ell\vec{v}_0,\dots,p_{k-1})\rightarrow(p_0+\ell\vec{v}_0,p_1+\ell\vec{v}_1,\dots,p_{k-1})\rightarrow(p_0+\ell\vec{v}_0,p_1+\ell\vec{v}_1,p_2+\ell\vec{v}_2,\dots,p_{k-1}),\)

and so on. We now give the details.

### Constructing a Steiner shortcut.

Let \(G_+=(V\cup V_+,E\cup E_+)\) be the Steiner shortcut for _G_. The vertex set _V_<sub>+</sub> is partitioned into a collection of _k_-1 disjoint layers _S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S_<sub>_k_-1</sub>, where _S<sub>i</sub>_ is the set of tuples (_i,(p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p_<sub>_k_-1</sub>)), each point \(p_1,\dots,p_{k-1}\in\mathbb{Z}^d\) being contained in the rectangle \((-(r+1)r\ell,(r+1)r\ell]^d\). Note that by definition, each _S<sub>i</sub>_ has the same number of vertices as each _L<sub>i,j</sub>_: |_S<sub>i</sub>_|=|_L<sub>i,j</sub>_|=_N_.

Recall that \(P\subset S\times L_{\ell,0}\), where \(S\subset L_{0,0}\) is in the first layer. We include in _E_<sub>+</sub> shortcut edges \(E_0\cup E_1\cup\cdots\cup E_{k-1}\) of the following types. For each \(s=((0,0),(p_0,\dots,p_{k-1}))\in S\) and each subdirection \(\vec{v}_0\in\mathcal{B}(r,d)\), we add edges of the following form to _E_<sub>0</sub>.<tbc>

\(\left(((0,0),(p_0,\dots,p_{k-1})),(1,(p_0+\ell\vec{v}_0,\dots,p_{k-1})\right)\in S\times S_1\)

<tbc>Likewise, for each index \(i\in[1,k-2]\), we include in \(E_i\subseteq S_i\times S_{i+1}\) all edges of the following form,<tbc>

\(\left((i,(p_0,\dots,p_i,\dots,p_{k-1})),(i+1,(p_0,\dots,p_i+\ell\vec{v}_i,\dots,p_{k-1}))\right)\in S_i\times S_{i+1}\)

<tbc>where \((i,(p_1,\dots,p_k))\in S_i\) and \(\vec{v}_i\in\mathcal{B}(r,d)\) is a critical subdirection. Finally, \(E_{k-1}\subseteq S_{k-1}\times L_{\ell,0}\) contains all edges of the following form.

\(\left((k-1,(p_0,\dots,p_{k-1})),((\ell,0),(p_1,\dots,p_k+\ell\vec{v}_{k-1}))\right)\in S_{k-1}\times L_{\ell,0},\)

where \((k-1,(p_1,\dots,p_k))\in S_{k-1}\) and \(\vec{v}_{k-1}\in\mathcal{B}(r,d)\) is a critical subdirection.

This completes the construction of our Steiner shortcut _G_<sub>+</sub>. We now argue it is a valid Steiner shortcut (i.e., it does not change the transitive closure restricted to \(V\times V\) ) and satisfies the size and distance claims of Theorem 2.2.

### Size of _G_<sub>+</sub>.

For each \(i\in[1,k-1]\), |_S<sub>i</sub>_|=_N_, so \(|V_+|=kN=\Theta(|V|/\ell)\). Each vertex in _V_<sub>+</sub> has indegree and outdegree at most \(|\mathcal{B}(r,d)|=\Delta\). We conclude that \(|E_+|=O(|V_+|\Delta)=O(|V|\Delta/\ell)\). Then \(|E_+|=O(|E|/\ell)=|E|n^{\Omega(1/(kd))}=|E|/n^{\Omega(1/k)}\) as claimed.

### Transitive closure and diameter.

We now verify that the transitive closure of _G_<sub>+</sub> restricted to the original vertices in _G_ is identical to the transitive closure of _G_. By construction, for any \((s,t)\in V\times V\) , any _s-t_ path in _G_<sub>+</sub> that uses Steiner vertices _V_<sub>+</sub> must be contained in \(W=S\times S_1\times S_2\times\cdots\times S_{k-1}\times L_{\ell,0}\). Let \(s\in S\subseteq L_{0,0}\) and \(t\in L_{\ell,0}\) be a pair of nodes such that there exists an _s-t_ path in _W_. By construction of \(E_+=E_0\cup\cdots\cup E_{k-1}\), this implies \(s=((0,0),p),t=((\ell,0),p+\ell\vec{v})\), where \(\vec{v}=(\vec{v}_0,\dots,\vec{v}_{k-1})\) are the critical subdirections corresponding to the edges along the path. In other words, \((s,t)\in P\) was already in the transitive closure of _G_. Conversely, any such \((s,t)\in P\) has a length-_k_ path in _W_. We conclude that _G_<sub>+</sub> is a valid reachability shortcut of _G_ and that dist<sub>_G_<sub>+</sub></sub>(_s,t_)=_k_ for \((s,t)\in P\).

## 3 Necessity of Thick Steiner Shortcuts

This section has two goals. First, we show that if ideal Steiner shortcuts exist with size _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> and diameter _m_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>, then they must be _thick_ on some graphs in the family G_<sub>k</sub>(c,d_). Second, we prove that a certain _randomized_ graph class \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(c,d,p)\) defined shortly is _strictly_ harder to shortcut than G_<sub>k</sub>(c,d_), and argue that it may in fact be sufficient to refute Conjecture 3.

Our first result is that G_<sub>k</sub>_ cannot be shortcut by any _t_-thick Steiner shortcut unless \(t\ge 0.99k\).

**Theorem 3.1.** _For_ \(k\ge 2\), \(t\le 0.99k\)_, and_ \(m=2^{\omega(k\mathrm{log}k)}\)_, every t-thick Steiner shortcut for the m-edge graph_ \(G\in\mathcal{G}_k\) _requires either_ \(m^{\Omega(1/k)}\) _diameter or_ \(m^{1+\Omega(1/k)}\) _edges._

Theorem 3.1 rules out _t_-thick Steiner shortcuts for _t=o_(log_n/_loglog_n_) and will be proved in Section 3.2. Note that Theorem 3.1’s constraint on _t_ is essentially sharp, as Theorem 2.2 shows that _k_-thick Steiner shortcuts can shortcut all the critical vertex pairs with length-_k_ paths.

### Noisy Version of G_<sub>k</sub>_.

We now introduce a noisy variant of the graph family G_<sub>k</sub>_, which we call \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(c,d,p)\). It is defined as \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(c,d,p)=\{\widetilde{G}(p)|G\in\mathcal{G}_k(c,d)\}\), where \(\widetilde{G}(p)\) denotes the (random) graph obtained from a given _G_ when deleting each edge independently with probability _p_. \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(c,d,p)\) is thus a family of random graphs that we obtain from the elements of G_<sub>k</sub>(c,d_) by deleting each edge independently with probability _p_. Here _p_ should not be thought of as an absolute constant, but a function of _c,d,r_ that is inversely proportional to the diameter of _G_.

Intuitively, the problem with G_<sub>k</sub>_ is that it has an extremely rigid structure that can be exploited by Steiner shortcuts. By randomly deleting edges, \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(c,d,p)\) destroys this structure. We highlight the following open problem, the resolution of which would either refute Conjecture 2 or contribute a significant step toward computing almost optimal Steiner shortcuts, either of which would be very exciting.

**Question 3.2.** _Are there parameters_ \(k\ge 2,c,d,p\) _for which any Steiner shortcut for an m-edge graph_ \(G\in\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(c,d,p)\) _cannot simultaneously have size m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> _and diameter m_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> ?

We report some partial progress towards answering Question 3.2 by showing, in a formal sense, that \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(c,d,p)\) is indeed harder to shortcut than G_<sub>k</sub>(c,d_). The following theorem, which will be proved in Section 3.3, shows that \(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(c,d,p)\) requires _t_-thick Steiner shortcuts for \(t>(1+\Omega(1))k\). In contrast, Theorem 3.1 applies only when \(t\le 0.99k\).

**Theorem 3.3.** _For_ \(k\ge 2\)_, there are parameters c,d,p such that with probability_ 1-1/poly(_m), every t-thick Steiner shortcut for the m-edge graph_ \(G\in\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_k(c,d,p)\) _requires either diameter_ \(m^{\Omega(1/k)}\) _or_ \(m^{1+\Omega(1/k)}\) _edges, provided that_ \(1.01t\le\frac{8}{7}k\) _and_ \(m=2^{\omega(k\mathrm{log}k)}\).

## 4 Generalized Shortcuts for Congestion and Length

Let us refer to shortcuts in previous sections as _reachability shortcuts_. In this section, we formalize the generalization of reachability shortcut that also preserves congestion and length in Section 4.1. Then, we explain why the construction of these shortcuts would imply algorithmic breakthroughs in parallel algorithms for shortest paths and maximum flow in Section 4.2. For convenience, we assume lengths and capacities are polynomially bounded integers in this section.

### 4.1 Formalization

Here, we define a notion of _length-constrained flow shortcuts_ (LC-flow shortcuts). This is a shortcut added to the graph so that every multi-commodity flow can be routed with approximately the same congestion and length, but all flow paths only require a small number of edges.

To formalize this, we need notation for multi-commodity flows. Let _G_=(_V,E_) be a graph with edge capacity \(c:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) and edge length \(\ell:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). A _(multi-commodity) flow F_ in<tbc>

<tbc>_G_ assigns value \(F(P)\ge 0\) for each directed path _P_ in _G_. We say that _P_ is a flow path of _F_ if _F(P)\>_0. The _congestion_ on edge _e_ of _F_ is \(\cong_F(e)=\frac{\sum_{e\in PF(P)}}{c(e)}\) and the congestion of _F_ is \(\cong_F=\mathrm{max}_{e\in E}\cong_F(e)\). The _length_ of _F_ is the maximum total length overall flow paths of _F_, i.e., \(\mathrm{max}_{P:F(P)>0}\ell(P)\). The _hopbound_ of _F_ is the maximum number of edges overall flow paths of _F_, i.e., max<sub>_P:F(P)\>_0</sub>|_E(P_)|. For any vertex set _U_, a _demand D on U_ assigns a value \(D(u,v)\ge 0\) for each vertex pair \((u,v)\in U\). The demand _D<sub>F</sub>_ routed by _F_ is defined as \(D_F(u,v):=\sum_{(u,v)\text{-path}_PF}F(P)\). We say that _D_ is routable with length \(\ell\), congestion \(\kappa\), and hopbound _h_ if there exists a flow _F_ with length \(\ell\), congestion \(\kappa\), and hopbound _h_ that routes _D_. When _D_ is routable in _G_ with congestion 1, we sometimes just say that _D_ is routable in _G_. With this, we are ready to define LC-flow shortcuts.

**Definition 4.1** (Length-Constrained Flow Shortcuts)**.** A shortcut \(G'=(V\cup V',E\cup E')\) is a _length-constrained flow shortcut of G_ with hopbound _h_,<sup>7</sup> congestion slack \(\kappa\), and length slack _s_ if:

1. Every demand on _V_ routable in _G_ with length \(\lambda\) and congestion 1 is routable in \(G'\) with length \(\lambda s\), congestion 1, and hopbound _h_, and<tbc>

2. Every demand on _V_ routable in \(G'\) with length \(\lambda\) and congestion 1 is routable in _G_ with length \(\lambda\) and congestion \(\kappa\).

The concept of LC-flow shortcut above was recently defined in undirected graphs \[HHL<sup>+</sup>24\]. They show that, for any _n_-vertex undirected graph _G_ with capacity and length at most poly(_n_) and a parameter _k_, there exists a flow shortcut \(G'\) with hopbound _h=O(k_), length slack _s=O(k_), congestion slack \(\mathrm{poly}(k\mathrm{log}n)n^{O(1/\sqrt{k})}\), and size \(|E'|\le n^{1+O(1/\sqrt{k})}\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{log}n)\). It is an interesting open problem if an LC-flow shortcut with non-trivial guarantee exists.

## Reachability Shortcuts, Distance Shortcuts, and Congestion Shortcuts.

Observe that a reachability shortcut is precisely an LC-flow shortcut when the constraints related to length and congestion in Definition 4.1 are removed.

We will use the terms _distance shortcut_ and _congestion shortcut_ to refer to an LC-flow shortcut when the respective constraint related to congestion and length in the definition of Definition 4.1 is removed.

More specifically, when focusing only on length, Definition 4.1 simplifies to distance shortcuts as follows. Let dist_<sub>G</sub>(s,t_) denote the distance from _s_ to _t_ in _G_. Let \(\mathrm{dist}_G^h(s,t)\) denote the minimum length of paths with hopbound _h_ from _s_ to _t_ in _G_.

**Definition 4.2** (Distance Shortcuts)**.** A shortcut \(G'=(V\cup V',E\cup E')\) is a _distance shortcut of G_ with hopbound _h_ and length slack _s_ if, for every vertex pair \((s,t)\in V\times V\) ,

1. If \(\mathrm{dist}_G(s,t)\le\lambda\), then \(\mathrm{dist}_{G^\prime}^h(s,t)\le\lambda s\) and<tbc>

2. If \(\mathrm{dist}_{G^\prime}(s,t)\le\lambda\), then \(\mathrm{dist}_G(s,t)\le\lambda\).

When focusing only on congestion, Definition 4.1 simplifies to congestion shortcuts as follows:

**Definition 4.3** (Congestion Shortcuts)**.** A shortcut \(G=(V\cup V',E\cup E')\) is a _congestion shortcut of G_ with hop bound _h_ and congestion slack \(\kappa\) if

1. Every demand on _V_ routable in _G_ is routable in \(G'\) with hopbound _h_, and<tbc>

2. Every demand on _V_ routable in \(G'\) is routable in _G_ with congestion \(\kappa\).<tbc>

<sup>7</sup>The hopbound in this section has the same purpose as the diameter in previous sections. We change to our terminology to hopbound to avoid confusion, because the graph here has edge lengths.

## 4.2 Exact Shortest Paths via \((1+\epsilon)\)-Approximate Distance Shortcuts

In this section, we observe that a near-optimal parallel algorithm for constructing a distance shortcut with length slack (1+_o_(1/log_n_)) would imply a near-optimal parallel algorithm for _exact_ single-source shortest paths with \(\tilde{O}(m)\) work and polylog(_n_) depth.

In the SSSP problem, given a graph _G_ and a vertex _s_, we need to output the exact distance _d(u_) from _s_ to every other vertex _u_ in _G_. For \(\alpha\)-approximate SSSP, we are given a graph _G_ and a vertex _s_, output an approximate distance \(\tilde{d}(u)\) from _s_ to every other vertex _u_ in _G_, such that \(d(u)\le\tilde{d}(u)\le\alpha d(u)\).

The reduction from parallel exact SSSP to distance shortcut construction follows from combining tools from \[KS97\] and \[RHM<sup>+</sup>23b\].

**Theorem 4.4.** _For any_ \(n,m,m',h\)_, suppose there is an algorithm_ A _which takes an O(m)-edge O(n)- vertex directed graph and computes a distance shortcut of hopbound O(h), length slack_ (1+_o_(1/log_n_)) _and size_ \(O(m')\)_. Then, there is an algorithm computing exact SSSP of an m-edges n-vertex directed graph with_ \(\tilde{O}\left(1\right)\) _calls to_ A_, with additional_ \(\tilde{O}\left(m+m'\right)\) _work and_ \(\tilde{O}\left(h\right)\) _depth._

In undirected graphs, there exist distance shortcuts of hopbound _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>, length slack (1+1/log<sup>2</sup>_n_) and size _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> (e.g. \[Coh00, HP19\]). Moreover, \[EN19\] showed how to construct them in _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> work and _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> depth.

If this can be generalized to directed graphs even when the shortcut size is _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>, then Theorem 4.4 would imply an exact SSSP algorithm with _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> work and _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> depth.

**Corollary 4.5.** _Suppose there is an algorithm that, given O(m)-edge O(n)-vertex directed graph, computes a distance shortcut of hopbound n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>_, length slack_ (1+_o_(1/log_n_))_, and size m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>_. Then, there is an algorithm for computing exact SSSP in an m-edge n-vertex directed graphs in m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> _work and n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> _depth._

Indeed, in directed graphs, the state-of-the-art is still far from this goal, because the problem is even harder than reachability shortcut. There exist distance shortcuts of hopbound \(\tilde{O}(n^{1/3})\), length slack \((1+\epsilon)\) and size \(\tilde{O}(n/\epsilon^2)\) \[BW23\], but they require large polynomial time to construct. \[CFR20\] showed a parallel algorithm with \(\tilde{O}(m/\epsilon^2)\) work and _n_<sup>0.5+_o_(1)</sup> depth to construct a distance shortcut of hopbound _n_<sup>1/2+_o_(1)</sup>, length slack \((1+\epsilon)\) and size \(\tilde{O}(n/\epsilon^2)\).

Note that, since Theorem 4.4 is a _work-efficient_ reduction, any improvement to the _n_<sup>1/2+_o_(1)</sup> hopbound of \[CFR20\] would immediately improve the start-of-the-art for parallel exact SSSP problem which currently requires \(\tilde{O}(m)\) work and _n_<sup>1/2+_o_(1)</sup> depth \[CFR20, RHM<sup>+</sup>23b\].

**Proof of Theorem 4.4**

_Proof._ We first present an algorithm for computing (1+_o_(1/log_n_))-approximate SSSP in an _O(m_)-edge, _O(n_)-vertex directed graph with 1 call to A and additional \(\widetilde{O}\left(m+m'\right)\) time and \(\widetilde{O}\left(h\right)\) depth. We then show how to solve exact SSSP of an _m_-edge _n_-vertex graph using \(\widetilde{O}\left(1\right)\) calls to the approximation algorithm with additional \(\widetilde{O}\left(m\right)\) work and \(\widetilde{O}\left(h\right)\) depth. Combining the two reductions finishes the proof.

### Approximate SSSP.

Given a directed _G_ with _O(m_) edges and _O(n_) vertices, we first compute a distance shortcut of size \(O(m')\), denoted by \(G'=(V\cup V',E\cup E')\). We will apply \[KS97, Lemma 3.2\], to \(G'\), which we state as follows.

**Lemma 4.6** (\[KS97, Lemma 3.2\])**.** _Given a directed graph G, a vertex u and parameters_ \(h,\epsilon\)_, there is an algorithm computing a h_-limited \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximate shortest path \(\tilde{d}_h\) _defined as_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\forall v\in V,d_h(v)\le\tilde{d}_h(v)\le(1+\epsilon)\cdot d_h(v)\) _where d<sub>h</sub>(v_) _is the shortest path distance restricted to only using h edges, in_ \(\tilde{O}\left(mk\epsilon^{-1}\right)\) _work and_ \(\tilde{O}\left(k\epsilon^{-1}\right)\) _depth._

We can compute an _h_-limited (1+_o_(1/log_n_))-approximate shortest path distances \(\{\tilde{d}^{G^\prime}(u)\}_{u\in V}\) in \(\tilde{O}\left(m+m'\right)\) work and \(\tilde{O}\left(h\right)\) depth (by setting the parameter _p=m/k_ in their paper). We use \(\{\tilde{d}^{G^\prime}(u)\}_{u\in V}\) as the output. This finishes the algorithm description, which uses 1 call to A with additional \(\tilde{O}\left(m\right)\) work and \(\tilde{O}\left(1\right)\) depth.

In their definition, a _h_-limited (1+_o_(1/log_n_)-approximate shortest path distances \(\{\tilde{d}_h^{G^\prime}(u)\}_{u\in V}\) satisfies that \(d_h^{G^\prime}(u)\le\tilde{d}_h^{G^\prime}(u)\le(1+o(1/logn))d_h^{G^\prime}(u)\), where \(d_h^{G^\prime}(u)\) is the shortest path distance restricted to only using _h_ edges. Thus, we have \(d^G(u)\le\tilde{d}_h^{G^\prime}(u)\le(1+o(1/logn))(1+o(1/logn))d^G(u)\), which means \(\tilde{d}_h^{G^\prime}(u)\) is a (1+_o_(1/log_n_))- approximate distance.

The following lemma is a direct implication of Theorem 1.7 and Lemma 3.1 in \[RHM<sup>+</sup>23b\],

**Lemma 4.7** (\[RHM<sup>+</sup>23b, Theorem 1.7 and Lemma 3.1\])**.** _Given a directed graph G, a source_ \(s\in V(G)\)_, there is an algorithm computing the exact distance from s to every node in G, using_ \(\tilde{O}\left(1\right)\) _calls to a_ (1+_O_(1/log_n_))_-approximate distance oracle_ O _on directed graphs and an additional_ \(\tilde{O}\left(m\right)\) _work and_ \(\tilde{O}\left(1\right)\) _depth._<sup>8</sup>

## 4.3 Parallel Exact Max Flow via \(\tilde{O}(1)\)-Approximate Congestion Shortcuts

In this section, we observe that a near-optimal parallel algorithm for constructing a congestion shortcut with congestion slack polylog(_n_) (together with an embedding algorithm defined below) would imply a near-optimal parallel algorithm for _exact_ maximum flow with \(\tilde{O}(m)\) work and polylog(_n_) depth.

**Definition 4.8** (Backward Mapping)**.** For a shortcut algorithm A which outputs a shortcut \(G'\) of the input graph _G_=(_V,E_), a _backward mapping algorithm_ for A takes input _G_ and \(G'\) generated by A, along with a flow \(F'\) in \(G'\) with congestion 1, outputs a flow _F_ in _G_ routing the same demand as \(F'\) with congestion \(\kappa\).

The reduction from parallel exact max flow to congestion shortcut construction follows quite straightforwardly by repeatedly solving approximate max flow on the residual graph.

**Theorem 4.9.** _Given_ \(n,m,m',h,\kappa\)_, suppose there is an algorithm_ A _which takes an O(m)-edge O(n)- vertex directed graph and computes a congestion shortcut of hopbound O(h), congestion slackness_ \(\kappa\) _and size_ \(O(m')\)_, along with a corresponding embedding algorithm_ \(\mathcal{A}'\) _for_ A_, then there is an algorithm computing exact max flow with_ \(\tilde{O}\left(\kappa\right)\) _calls to_ A _and_ \(\mathcal{A}'\) _and additional_ \(\tilde{O}\left(\kappa\cdot\mathrm{poly}(h)\cdot(m+m')\right)\) _work and_ \(\tilde{O}\left(\kappa\cdot\mathrm{poly}(h)\right)\) _depth._

In undirected graphs, congestion shortcuts with near-optimal quality follows from _tree flow sparsifiers_ defined as follows.

<sup>8</sup>One might notice that Lemma 4.1 in \[KS97\] is also about reducing exact shortcut path to approximate shortest path oracles. However, they require a stronger approximate shortest path oracle: The approximate distance must be an exact distant on the shortcut \(G'\). Thus, it cannot be used here.

**Definition 4.10.** A _tree flow sparsifier T_ of _G_ with congestion slack \(\kappa\) is such that

1. The set of leaves of _T_ corresponds to _V(G_).<tbc>

2. Every demand on _V(G_) routable in _G_ is routable in _T_<tbc>

3. Every demand on _V(G_) routable in _T_ is routable in _G_ with congestion \(\kappa\).

Clearly from the definition, a tree flow sparsifier with depth _d_ and congestion slack \(\kappa\) is a congestion shortcut with congestion slack \(\kappa\), hopbound 2_d_, and size _O(n_). There exists a tree flow sparsifier with depth _O_(log_n_) and congestion slack _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_n_loglog_n_) \[HHR03\]. Moreover, there is a parallel algorithm that construct a tree flow sparsifier with depth _O_(log_n_) and congestion slack _O_(log<sup>9</sup>_n_) in \(\tilde{O}(m)\) work and polylog(_n_) depth \[AKL<sup>+</sup>24\].

If this can be generalized to directed graphs even when the shortcut size is \(\tilde{O}(m)\), then Theorem 4.9 would imply an exact max flow algorithm with \(\tilde{O}(m)\) work and polylog(_n_) depth.

**Corollary 4.11.** _Suppose there is an algorithm that, given O(m)-edge O(n)-vertex directed graph, computes a congestion shortcut of hopbound_ polylog(_n), length slack_ polylog(_n), and size_ \(\tilde{O}(m)\)_. Then, there is an algorithm for computing exact max flow in an m-edge n-vertex directed graphs in_ \(\tilde{O}(m)\) _work and_ polylog(_n_) _depth._

Unfortunately, there is no prior work on this and we leave it an interesting open problem.

**Proof of Theorem 4.9**

_Proof._ We first give an algorithm computing approximate max flow which routes a feasible flow whose value is at least \(1/2\kappa\) times the optimal value on the input graph. Then show how to turn it into an exact max flow algorithm.

**Approximate max flow.** We first use A to compute a congestion shortcut on _G_, denoted by \(E'\). Let \(G'=G\cup E'\). We will use Theorem 3.1 (1) of \[HHS23\], stated as follows.

**Lemma 4.12** (Theorem 3.1 (1) of \[HHS23\])**.** _Given a directed graph G with edge capacities and unit edge length, length bound_ \(h\ge 1\)_, approximation parameter_ \(\epsilon>0\)_, and source and sink_ \(s,t\in V\)_, there is an algorithm computing a_ \(1-\epsilon\) _approximate maximum h-length flow, in the sense that the flow value is at least_ \(1-\epsilon\) _times the maximum h-length flow from s to t in G. The algorithm takes_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(m\cdot h^{17}\cdot\frac{1}{\epsilon^9}\right)\) _work and_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(h^{17}\cdot\frac{1}{\epsilon^9}\right)\) _depth._

We use Lemma 4.12 with parameter \(\epsilon=1/2\), _h_ the same as our _h_, and the digraph the same as \(G'\) with unit length. The guarantee for the output is a flow \(F'\), which is a \(1-\epsilon\) approximation for maximum _h_-length flow, which, in our case, is the maximum flow with hop bound _h_ since the graph has unit length. Then, we call the backward mapping algorithm A to turn \(F'\) into a flow _F_ on _G_ with congestion \(\kappa\). To make _F_ feasible, we scale the flow on each edge down by a factor of \(\kappa\), and denote the final flow as \(F/\kappa\). According to Definition 4.1, every flow on _G_ corresponds to a feasible flow on \(G'\) with hop bound _h_ and the same value. Thus, \(F'\) has a value of at least 1/2 times the max flow value on _G_, which implies that \(F/\kappa\) is a \(1/2\kappa\) approximate max flow on _G_.

The algorithm takes an input graph of _m_ edges and _n_ vertices, uses 1 call to A and \(\mathcal{A}'\), and additional \(\widetilde{O}\left(\text{poly}(h)\cdot(m+m')\right)\) work and poly(_h_) depth using Lemma 4.12.

### Exact max flow.

If we have an algorithm computing \(\epsilon\)-approximate max flow (here \(\epsilon=1/2\kappa\)), then we can use a folklore reduction to get the exact max flow: iteratively compute approximate max flows on the residual graph. In \(\widetilde{O}\left(1/\epsilon\right)\) iterations the optimal flow value of the residual graph will be decreased to 1/poly(_n_). Notice that we can also apply the standard rounding algorithm (for example, see \[Coh95, §5\]) if we want to get an integer flow of the max flow value.

The algorithm uses \(\widetilde{O}\left(\kappa\right)\) calls to the approximate max flow algorithm, which corresponds to \(\widetilde{O}\left(\kappa\right)\) calls to \(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}'\), and additional \(\widetilde{O}\left(\kappa\cdot\mathrm{poly}(h)\cdot\left(m+m'\right)\right)\) work and \(\widetilde{O}\left(\kappa\cdot\mathrm{poly}(h)\right)\) depth.

## A Lower Bounds for \(m^{1-\epsilon}\)-Sized Steiner Shortcuts

In this section, we present a simple lower bound ruling out the existence of strongly sublinear Steiner reachability shortcuts with subpolynomial diameter.

**Theorem A.1.** _For every sufficiently small constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_, there exists an infinite family of n-node, m-edge directed graphs G, where_ \(m\in\left[n,n^{2-4\epsilon^{1/2}+\epsilon}\right]\)_, such that every Steiner reachability shortcut of G has size at least_ \(\tilde{\Omega}(m^{1-\epsilon})\) _or diameter at least_ \(\Omega(n^\epsilon)\).

Our lower bound argument will require the following lemma, which can be attributed to existing lower bounds for reachability preservers in \[AB24\].

**Lemma A.2** (cf. Theorem 13 of \[AB24\])**.** _For every sufficiently small_ \(\epsilon>0\)_, there exists an infinite family of n-node directed graphs G, each with an associated collection of directed paths_ P _in G with the following properties:_

1. \(|\mathcal{P}|\ge n^{2-4\epsilon^{1/2}}\),<tbc>

_2._ _each path_ \(P\in\mathcal{P}\) _has_ \(|P|=n^\epsilon\) _edges,_<tbc>

_3._ _paths in_ P _are pairwise edge-disjoint, and_<tbc>

_4._ _each path_ \(P\in\mathcal{P}\) _is the unique directed path between its endpoints in graph G._

Using Lemma A.2, we can directly prove Theorem A.1.

_Proof of Theorem A.1._ Let \(\epsilon>0\) be a sufficiently small constant and let _m_ be some function of _n_ such that \(m\in\left[n,n^{2-4\epsilon^{1/2}+\epsilon}\right]\). By Lemma A.2, there exists an infinite family of _n_-node directed graphs _G_, each with an associated collection of directed paths P in _G_ satisfying the properties in Lemma A.2. Since paths in P are pairwise edge-disjoint and each has length at least \(n^\epsilon\), we observe that

\(|E(G)|\ge|\mathcal{P}|n^\epsilon\ge n^{2-4\epsilon^{1/2}+\epsilon}.\)

We can ensure that \(|E(G)|=\Theta(m)\) by repeatedly removing paths in P from graph _G_ until we achieve the desired graph density. After performing this procedure, |_E(G_)|=_m_ and \(|\mathcal{P}|=mn^{-\epsilon}\ge m^{1-\epsilon}\), by Property 2 of Lemma A.2.

We will achieve our Steiner shortcut lower bound via an information theoretic argument. More specifically, we use graph _G_ to construct a graph family G of size |G|=2<sup>|P|</sup>. For each subset \(S\subseteq\mathcal{P}\), we define graph _G<sup>S</sup>_ as follows:

1. Initially, let _G<sup>S</sup>_:=_G_.<tbc>

2. For each path \(P\in\mathcal{P}-S\), remove every edge in _P_ from graph _G<sub>S</sub>_, so that \(G^S\leftarrow G^S-E(P)\).

Since paths in P are pairwise edge-disjoint in _G_ by Lemma A.2, a path \(P\in\mathcal{P}\) is contained in graph _G<sup>S</sup>_ if and only if \(P\in S\).

For each graph _G<sup>S</sup>_=(_V<sup>S</sup>,E<sup>S</sup>_) where \(S\subseteq\mathcal{P}\), let \(G_+^S=(V^S\cup V_+^S,E^S\cup E_+^S)\) be a Steiner shortcut graph of _G<sup>S</sup>_ with diameter at most \(n^\epsilon/2\) that minimizes \(|V_+^S|+|E_+^S|\). (Recall that the size of a Steiner shortcut graph is precisely \(|V_+^S|+|E_+^S|\).) We claim that one of these graphs \(G_+^S\) has size at least \(|V_+^S|+|E_+^S|\ge\tilde{\Omega}(m^{1-\epsilon})\).

For each \(S\subseteq\mathcal{P}\), let \(H_+^S=G_+^S-E^S\). This graph contains exactly the Steiner edges \(E_+^S\) in graph \(G_+^S\). We define the graph family G to be \(\mathcal{G}=\{H_+^S\}_{S\subseteq\mathcal{P}}\). Let \(x=max_{S\subseteq\mathcal{P}}|V_+^S|+|E_+^S|\). We observe that each graph \(H_+^S\in\mathcal{G}\) has at most _x+n_ vertices and at most _x_ edges. Now note that without loss of generality, we can interpret each directed graph \(H_+^S\in\mathcal{G}\) as a subgraph of a vertex-labeled, complete, directed graph with _x_ vertices. We denote this universal graph as \(\hat{G}\). Under this interpretation, \(H_+^S\subseteq\hat{G}\) for each \(H_+^S\in\mathcal{G}\).

Now we claim that for distinct sets of paths \(S,S'\subseteq\mathcal{P}\), we have that \(H_+^S\neq H_+^{S^\prime}\) (we say that \(H_+^S=H_+^{S^\prime}\) if both graphs correspond to the same subgraph of \(\hat{G}\), and we say that \(H_+^S\neq H_+^{S^\prime}\) otherwise). Since \(S\neq S'\), we may assume without loss of generality that there exists a path \(P\in S-S'\). Since \(G_+^S\) is a Steiner shortcut graph of _G<sup>S</sup>_ with diameter \(\le n^\epsilon/2\), and path _P_ has length \(|P|=n^\epsilon\), and path _P_ is a unique path in _G<sup>S</sup>_ by Property 4 of Lemma A.2, we conclude that there must exist a path in graph \(H_+^S=G_+^S-E^S\) between a pair of vertices (_s,t_) in the transitive closure of path _P_. On the other hand, no edge in path _P_ is contained in graph \(G^{S^\prime}\), i.e., \(E(P)\cap E^{S^\prime}=\emptyset\), so by Property 4 of Lemma A.2, there does not exist a path in graph \(G_+^{S^\prime}\) between<tbc>

<tbc>a pair of vertices (_s,t_) in the transitive closure of path _P_. We conclude that \(G_+^S\neq G_+^{S^\prime}\), as claimed. This implies that there are 2<sup>|P|</sup> distinct, vertex-labeled graphs in graph family G.

Finally, we observe that there are at most (_x+n_)<sup>2_x_</sup> distinct subgraphs of the universal graph \(\hat{G}\) with at most _x+n_ vertices and at most _x_ edges, so \((x+n)^{2x}\ge 2^{|\mathcal{P}|}\). Taking the log of both sides, we get \(xlog(x+n)\ge|\mathcal{P}|\), which implies that \(x\ge|\mathcal{P}|/log(|\mathcal{P}|)=\tilde{\Omega}(m^{1-\epsilon})\). Then by the definition of _x_, one of the Steiner shortcut graphs \(G_+^S\), where \(S\subseteq\mathcal{P}\), has size at least \(x=\tilde{\Omega}(m^{1-\epsilon})\). This completes the proof.

## B Reachability Shortcuts as OR-circuit Depth Reduction

In this section we will show that the existence of Steiner shortcuts for reachability is equivalent to the existence of a depth reduction for a certain class of Boolean circuits.

**Theorem B.1.** _Conjecture 2 is equivalent to Conjecture 3._

### Preliminaries.

A Boolean circuit is a directed acyclic graph with a set of source nodes _S_, called input gates, and a set of sink nodes _T_, called output gates. The input gates are labeled with binary variables _x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_, and the output gates are labeled with binary variables _y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,y<sub>n</sub>_.

Each non-source/sink node in the circuit computes a Boolean function (e.g., AND, OR, NOT). We will restrict our attention to circuits with only OR gates, which we refer to as OR-circuits. Our OR gates will have unbounded fan-in. We measure the size of a Boolean circuit by the number of edges it has. We define the depth of a circuit as the length of the longest path in the directed acyclic graph. We define the _diameter_ of a circuit as the largest distance between an input gate and an output gate in the directed acyclic graph.

The connection between reachability and OR-circuits can be summarized by the following observation.

**Observation B.2.** _Let C be an OR-circuit with input gates_ \(S\subseteq V(C)\) _and output gates_ \(T\subseteq V(C)\)_. Let_ \(t\in T\) _be an output gate labeled with binary variable_ \(y\in\{0,1\}\)_. Then output gate t returns the value y_=1 _if and only if there exists an input gate_ \(s\in S\) _such that s can reach t in C, and input gate s is labeled with a binary variable_ \(x\in\{0,1\}\) _that has the value x_=1.

We can now prove an equivalence between diameter-reducing Steiner shortcuts and the existence of diameter-reductions for OR-circuits.

**Lemma B.3.** _Let s(m_) _and d(m_) _be functions such that s(m),d(m_)=_O_(poly(_m_))_. Then the following two statements are equivalent:_

(_1)_ _Every directed graph on n nodes and m edges admits a Steiner reachability shortcut with s(m_)+_O(m+n_) _additional edges and diameter d(m_)+_O_(1).<tbc>

_(2)_ _Let_ \(f:\{0,1\}^n\mapsto\{0,1\}^n\) _be a multi-output Boolean function that can be computed by a Boolean_ OR_-circuit with m edges. Then f can be computed by an_ OR_-circuit with s(m_)+_O(m+n_) _edges and diameter d(m_)+_O_(1).

_Proof._ We will prove each direction separately.

<tbc>(1) \(\Longrightarrow\) (2).

Let \(f:\{0,1\}^n\mapsto\{0,1\}^n\) be a multi-output Boolean function that can be computed by a Boolean OR-circuit with _m_ edges. Let _G_ be the DAG of the Boolean circuit computing _f_, where |_E(G_)|=_m_. Graph _G_ has source nodes \(S\subseteq V(G)\) and sink nodes \(T\subseteq V(G)\), corresponding to input gates and output gates respectively, such that |_S_|=|_T_|=_n_.

Let _H_ be a Steiner reachability shortcut of graph _G_, with \(V(G)\subseteq V(H)\) and \(E(G)\subseteq E(H)\). We may assume without loss of generality that _H_ is a DAG, by contracting all strongly connected components (SCCs) in _H_. This operation will not contract any nodes in _S_ or _T_. Additionally, we can also assume wlog that every source node in _H_ is contained in _S_, and every sink node in _H_ is contained in _T_. Consequently, we can interpret _H_ as an OR-circuit with input gates _S_ and output gates _T_. We claim that circuit _H_ computes function _f_ and satisfies Statement (2).

By Statement (1), |_E(H_)|=_s(m_)+_O(m+n_) and _H_ has depth _d(m_)+_O_(1), as desired. Since _H_ is a Steiner reachability shortcut of _G_, for all \((s,t)\in S\times T\), node _s_ can reach node _t_ in _G_ if and only if node _s_ can reach node _t_ in _H_. Then by Observation B.2, circuit _H_ must compute the same Boolean function as circuit _G_. Then circuit _H_ computes function _f_, as claimed.

(2) \(\Longrightarrow\) (1).

Let _G_ be an _n_-node, _m_-edge directed graph. We may assume wlog that \(m\ge n-1\). Likewise, we may assume wlog that _G_ is a directed acyclic graph, via the following procedure. Contract every SCC in _G_ to obtain a DAG \(G'\). Then a simple argument will show that _G_ has a Steiner reachability shortcut with _s(m_)+_O(m+n_) additional edges and depth _d(m_)+_O_(1) if and only if \(G'\) has one as well.

We will convert DAG _G_ into a circuit _C_ as follows. Let \(v_1,\dots,v_n\in V(G)\) be the nodes of graph _G_. We will define sets of new nodes _S_={_s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>n</sub>_} and _T_={_t_<sub>1</sub>_,...,t<sub>n</sub>_}. Nodes _S_ and _T_ will become the input gates and output gates, respectively, of _C_. Let the vertex set of _C_ be \(V(C)=V(G)\cup S\cup T\). We define the edge set _E(C_) of _C_ to be

\(E(C)=E(G)\cup\bigcup_{i\in[1,n]}\{(s_i,v_i),(v_i,t_i)\}.\)

Notice that _C_ is a directed acyclic graph with source nodes _S_ and sink nodes _T_. Consequently, we can interpret _C_ as an OR-circuit with input gates _S_ and output gates _T_. We label node _s<sub>i</sub>_ with binary variable _x<sub>i</sub>_, and we label node _t<sub>i</sub>_ with binary variable _y<sub>i</sub>_, for \(i\in[1,n]\). Let \(f:\{0,1\}^n\mapsto\{0,1\}^n\) denote the Boolean function that circuit _C_ computes.

Let \(m'=|E(C)|=m+2n\). By Statement (2), there exists an OR-circuit \(C'\) with sources _S_ and sinks _T_, such that

• circuit \(C'\) computes function _f_,<tbc>

• circuit \(C'\) has \(s(m')+O(m'+n)=s(m)+O(m+n)\) edges, and<tbc>

• circuit \(C'\) has depth \(d(m')+O(1)=d(m)+O(1)\).

We convert circuit \(C'\) into a Steiner reachability shortcut _H_ of graph _G_ as follows. Let _V(H_) be the disjoint union of \(V(C')\) and the vertex set _V(G_) of _G_. We define the edge set _E(H_) of _H_ to be

\(E(H)=E(C')\bigcup_{i\in[1,n]}\{(v_i,s_i),(t_i,v_i)\}.\)

We claim that graph _H_ is a Steiner reachability shortcut of _G_ and satisfies Statement (1).

We will need the following observation about circuit \(C'\). Fix an \(i\in[1,n]\), and let _x<sub>i</sub>_=1 and _x<sub>j</sub>_=0 for \(j\neq i\). Let _f(x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_)=(_y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,y<sub>n</sub>_). Then by Observation B.2, for any \(j\in[1,n]\), we have that _y<sub>j</sub>_=1 if and only if _v<sub>i</sub>_ can reach _v<sub>j</sub>_ in _G_. Since circuit \(C'\) computes function _f_, we<tbc>

conclude that for all \((s_i,t_j)\in S\times T\), we have that _s<sub>i</sub>_ can reach _t<sub>j</sub>_ in \(C'\) if and only if _v<sub>i</sub>_ can reach _v<sub>j</sub>_ in graph _G_.

We will first show that graph _H_ preserves the reachability relation of _G_ between vertices in \(V(G)\times V(G)\). Suppose that node _v<sub>i</sub>_ can reach node _v<sub>j</sub>_ in graph _G_. Then since we added edges (_v<sub>i</sub>,s<sub>i</sub>_) and (_t<sub>j</sub>,v<sub>j</sub>_) to graph _H_, the above observation immediately implies that _v<sub>i</sub>_ can reach _v<sub>j</sub>_ in graph _H_.

Now suppose that _v<sub>i</sub>_ can reach _v<sub>j</sub>_ in graph _H_; we claim that _v<sub>i</sub>_ can reach _v<sub>j</sub>_ in graph _G_ as well. Let _P_ be a \(v_i\rightsquigarrow v_j\) path in graph _H_. We can write path _P_ as a concatenation of paths

\(P=P_1\circ\cdots\circ P_k,\)

where, for each \(\ell\in[1,k]\), subpath \(P_\ell\) is internally vertex-disjoint from _V(G_). For each \(\ell\in[1,k]\), let subpath \(P_\ell\) be an \(x_\ell\rightsquigarrow x_{\ell+1}\) path, where \(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}\in V(G)\), _x_<sub>1</sub>=_v<sub>i</sub>_, and _x_<sub>_k_+1</sub>=_v<sub>j</sub>_. Notice that since path \(P_\ell\) is internally vertex-disjoint from _V(G_), path \(P_\ell\) is a path in circuit \(C'\) as well, for all \(\ell\in[1,k]\). Then by our earlier observation about circuit \(C'\), we must have that \(x_\ell\) can reach \(x_{\ell+1}\) in _G_. We have shown that \(x_\ell\) can reach \(x_{\ell+1}\) in _G_ for all \(\ell\in[1,k]\), so by the transitivity of the reachability relation, we must have that _x_<sub>1</sub>=_v<sub>i</sub>_ can reach _x_<sub>_k_+1</sub>=_v<sub>j</sub>_ in _G_. We have shown that _H_ preserves the reachability relation of _G_ between vertices in \(V(G)\times V(G)\).

Finally, we quickly observe that \(|E(H)|=|E(C')|+2n=s(m)+O(m+n)\), and _H_ has diameter _d(m_)+_O_(1), as claimed in Statement (2).

With Lemma B.3 in hand, we can now prove that our conjecture for low-depth Steiner shortcuts (Conjecture 2) is equivalent to the conjecture for low-depth OR-circuits (Conjecture 3).

**Theorem B.1.** _Conjecture 2 is equivalent to Conjecture 3._

_Proof._ First, notice that if a Boolean OR-circuit has depth _d_, then it also has diameter _d_. Therefore, by Lemma B.3, if Conjecture 3 is true, then every directed graph on _n_ nodes and _m_ edges admits a Steiner reachability shortcut with \(\widetilde{O}(m)\) additional edges and diameter polylog(_n_), so Conjecture 2 is true as well.

What remains is to prove that Conjecture 2 implies Conjecture 3. If Conjecture 2 is true, then by Lemma B.3 every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\mapsto\{0,1\}^n\) that can be computed by a Boolean OR-circuit _C_ with size _s_<sub>1</sub> can also be computed by an OR-circuit with size \(s_2=\widetilde{O}(s_1)\) and diameter _d=O_(polylog(_n_)). We will now convert circuit _C_ into a circuit _C_<sup>∗</sup> with _depth O(d_) by a simple layering operation. Let _S_ denote the set of input gates of _C_, let _T_ denote the output gates of _C_, and let _V_ denote the set of OR gates in _C_. We will make _d_ copies of set _V_ , which we denote _V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>d</sub>_. Sets _V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>d</sub>_ will be the new OR gates in our new OR-circuit _C_<sup>∗</sup>. For each \(v\in V\) , we let \(v_i\in V_i\) denote the copy of _v_ in _V<sub>i</sub>_. We define the edge set of circuit _C_<sup>∗</sup> as follows:

• For each edge \((x,y)\in S\times V\) in circuit _C_, add edge \((x,y_1)\in S\times V_1\) to _C_<sup>∗</sup>.<tbc>

• For each edge \((x,y)\in V\times T\) in circuit _C_, add edge \((x_d,y)\in V_d\times T\) to _C_<sup>∗</sup>.<tbc>

• For each edge \((x,y)\in S\times T\) in circuit _C_, add edge \((x,y)\in S\times T\) to _C_<sup>∗</sup>.<tbc>

• For each edge \((x,y)\in V\times V\) , add edge \((x_i,y_{i+1})\in V_i\times V_{i+1}\) to _C_<sup>∗</sup> for every \(i\in[1,d-1]\).<tbc>

• For each \(v\in V\) and each \(i\in[1,d-1]\), add the edge \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in V_i\times V_{i+1}\) to _C_<sup>∗</sup>.

This completes the definition of the new circuit _C_<sup>∗</sup>.

We now quickly verify that circuit _C_<sup>∗</sup> computes the same function as _C_. Notice that an input gate \(s\in S\) can reach an output gate \(t\in T\) in circuit _C_ if and only if there is an (_s,t_)-path _P_=(_s,v_<sup>1</sup>_,v_<sup>2</sup>_,...,v<sup>k</sup>,t_) in _C_ of length at most _d_. If _P_ exists in _C_, then circuit _C_<sup>∗</sup> must contain the<tbc>

(_s,t_)-path \(P^*=(s,v_1^1,v_2^2,\dots,v_k^k,v_{k+1}^k,\dots,v_d^k,t)\). Likewise, if there exists an (_s,t_)-path _P_<sup>∗</sup> in _C_<sup>∗</sup>, then there exists an (_s,t_)-path _P_ in _C_. Then by Observation B.2, we conclude that circuit _C_ and circuit _C_<sup>∗</sup> compute the same binary function.

Finally, observe that circuit _C_<sup>∗</sup> has depth _O(d_)=_O_(polylog(_n_)) since every path in _C_<sup>∗</sup> can pass through at most one vertex in each layer _V<sub>i</sub>_ for \(i\in[1,d]\). Likewise, circuit _C_<sup>∗</sup> has size at most \(s_2\le s_1d=\widetilde{O}(s_1)\), since every edge in circuit _C_ is copied at most _d_ times in _C_<sup>∗</sup>.

## C Steiner Shortcut for the Lower Bound of \[VXX24\]

Before presenting our Steiner shortcut for the lower bound construction of \[VXX24\], we first give a sketch of its construction and relevant properties.

<tbc>\(L_i=\{i\}\times[1,4r]\times[1,4r]\times[1,4r^2].\)<tbc>

Let _v_<sub>0</sub>_,...,v_<sub>2_r_-1</sub> be a sequence of vectors where<tbc>

<tbc>\(v_i=(1,0,\sigma_{i/2})\)<tbc>

<tbc>for every even \(i\in[0,2r-1]\), and<tbc>

<tbc>\(v_i=(0,1,\sigma_{(i-1)/2})\)<tbc>

<tbc>for every odd \(i\in[0,2r-1]\).<tbc>

<tbc>For every \(i\in[0,2r-1]\) and every point \(x\in[4r]\times[4r]\times[4r^2]\), we add the edge \((i,x)\rightarrow(i+1,x)\) to edge set _E(G_), and we add the edge \((i,x)\rightarrow(i+1,x+v_i)\) to _E(G_) if \((i+1,x+v_i)\in L_{i+1}\) is a valid point in layer _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub>.<sup>9</sup><tbc>

• **Critical Paths** P**.** We define a collection P of paths in graph _G_. Towards this goal, we first define a set of source nodes \(S\subseteq L_0\). Specifically, we choose _S_ to be<tbc>

<tbc>\(S=\{0\}\times[2r]\times[2r]\times[2r^2]\subseteq L_0.\)<tbc>

<tbc>For each node \(s\in S\) and each choice of tuple \((d_1,d_2)\in[r]\times[r]\), we will define a critical path \(P_{d_1,d_2}^s\in\mathcal{P}\) that starts at node \(s\in L_0\) and ends at a node in _L_<sub>2_r_</sub>. <tbc>\(f_d(i)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\sigma_i & \sigma_i<d \\
0 & \text{else}
\end{array}\right.\)<tbc>

<tbc>We are now ready to define our critical paths P. Fix a node \(s\in S\) and a tuple \((d_1,d_2)\in[r]\times[r]\). We iteratively define a path \(P_{d_1,d_2}^s\) starting at _s_ and ending at a node in _L_<sub>2_r_</sub>. We now specify the edge that path \(P_{d_1,d_2}^s\) takes between layers _L<sub>i</sub>_ and _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub>, where \(i\in[0,2r-1]\).<tbc>

<sup>9</sup>The edge set _E(G_) is constructed using permutation \(\sigma\) to ensure Property 3 of Lemma C.1.

<tbc>\((i,x,y,z)\rightarrow(i+1,x+1,y,z+f_{d_1}(i/2)).\)<tbc>

**-** If \(i\equiv 1mod2\), then path \(P_{d_1,d_2}^s\) takes an edge of the form<tbc>

<tbc>\((i,x,y,z)\rightarrow(i+1,x,y+1,z+f_{d_2}((i-1)/2).\)<tbc>

We state without proof several properties of this graph construction.

**Lemma C.1** (cf. Proposition 5.1 of \[VXX24\])**.** _Graph G and paths_ P _have the following properties:_

1. \(|V(G)|=\Theta(r^5)\), \(|E(G)|=\Theta(r^5)\)_, and_ \(|\mathcal{P}|=\Theta(r^6)\).<tbc>

_2._ _(Uniqueness.) Every critical path in_ P _is the unique path between its endpoints in G._<tbc>

_3._ _(Low Overlap.) Any path_ \(\sigma\) _in G of length at most_ \(s\le 2r\) _is contained in at most O_((_r/s_)<sup>2</sup>) _distinct critical paths in_ P.

This graph construction of \[VXX24\] implies a polynomial lower bound on the diameter of _O(m_)-size shortcuts. We summarize this property of _G,_P in the following theorem.

**Theorem C.2** (cf. Theorem 1.3 of \[VXX24\])**.** _Fix a constant c\>_0_. Let_ \(H\subseteq TC(G)\) _be a shortcut set of G of size_ \(|H|\le c\cdot|E(G)|\)_. If construction parameter r of G,_P _is chosen to be sufficiently large, then there must exist an_ \(s\rightsquigarrow t\) _path_ \(P\in\mathcal{P}\) _such that_ \(\mathrm{dist}_{G\cup H}(s,t)=\Omega(r)=\Omega(|V(G)|^{1/5})\)_. Consequently, for any O(m)-size shortcut set_ \(H\subseteq TC(G)\)_, graph_ \(G\cup H\) _has diameter_ \(\Omega(n^{1/5})\).

The proof of Theorem C.2 uses a potential function argument which shows that every shortcut edge in _H_ can only decrease the lengths of paths in P by a small amount; intuitively, this follows from the low overlap property of paths in P stated in Lemma C.1.

## C.2 Steiner Shortcut to \[VXX24\]

We will now give a Steiner shortcut for the lower bound construction of \[VXX24\]. This Steiner shortcut rules out the possibility of extending Theorem C.2 to Steiner reachability shortcut sets via the argument used in \[VXX24\]. Formally, we will prove the following theorem about the graph _G_ and set of paths P corresponding to the lower bound construction of \[VXX24\].

**Theorem C.3** (Steiner Shortcut for \[VXX24\] Construction)**.** _Graph G and set of paths_ P _admit a Steiner reachability shortcut set H such that_

1. _H has O(r_<sup>4</sup>)=_O_(|_V(G_)|_/r_) _Steiner nodes and O(r_<sup>5</sup>)=_O_(|_E(G_)|) _edges, and_<tbc>

_2._ _For every_ \(s\rightsquigarrow t\) _path_ \(P\in\mathcal{P}\)_, there exists an_ \(s\rightsquigarrow t\) _path of length two in_ \(G\cup H\).<tbc>

## Construction of _H_.

The additional Steiner nodes in our Steiner reachability shortcut set _H_ will correspond to a collection of points in a three-dimensional grid. Specifically, we define a set of Steiner nodes _W_ to be

\(W=\{-1\}\times\{1,4r\}\times\{1,4r\}\times[1,4r^2].\)

(We add the -1 in the first coordinate of _W_ to distinguish the vertices in _W_ from the vertices in _V(G_).) The edge set _E(H_) of our Steiner shortcut will satisfy \(E(H)\subseteq(L_0\times W)\cup(W\times L_{2r})\).

Before we can define _E(H_), we need to introduce some new definitions. For every \(d\in[r]\) and every \(i\in\{1,2\}\), we define integer \(z_d^i\ge 0\) as follows:

\(z_d^1=\sum_{j\in[0,r-1]}f_d(2j)\text{and}z_d^2=\sum_{j\in[0,r-1]}f_d(2j+1).\)

Using integers \(z_d^i\), we are now ready to construct _E(H_).

• For every node \((0,x,y,z)\in S\) and every \(d\in[r]\), add the edge<tbc>

<tbc>\((0,x,y,z)\rightarrow\big(-1,x+r,y,z+z_d^1\big)\)<tbc>

<tbc>to _E(H_) if \(\big(-1,x+r,y,z+z_d^1\big)\in W\) is a valid point in _W_.<tbc>

• For every node \((-1,x,y,z)\in W\) and every \(d\in[r]\), add the edge<tbc>

<tbc>\((-1,x,y,z)\rightarrow\big(2r,x,y+r,z+z_d^2\big)\)<tbc>

<tbc>to _E(H_) if \(\big(2r,x,y+r,z+z_d^2\big)\in L_{2r}\) is a valid node in layer _L_<sub>2_r_</sub>.

This completes the construction of Steiner shortcut set _H_ and additional edges _E(H_).

## Analysis of _H_.

First we will bound the number of Steiner nodes in _W_ and the number of additional edges _E(H_) in our Steiner shortcut set. We observe that |_W_|=4<sup>3</sup>_r_<sup>4</sup>=_O(r_<sup>4</sup>), as claimed. Additionally, we observe that the total number of edges in our Steiner shortcut is at most

\(|E(H)|\le|S|\cdot r+|W|\cdot d\le 2^7r^5=O(r^5),\)

as claimed.

We next verify that _H_ is a valid Steiner reachability shortcut set, i.e., that the reachability relation between nodes in _V(G_) remains the same in \(G\cup H\). Let \(u,v\in V(G)\) be nodes such that path (_u,w,v_) exists in graph \(G\cup H\) for some \(w\in W\). Then we claim that _u_ can reach _v_ in _G_ as well. Let _u_=(0_,x,y,z_). We can write \(u\rightarrow w\rightarrow v\) as<tbc>

\((0,x,y,z)\rightarrow(-1,x+r,y,z+z_{d_1}^1)\rightarrow(2r,x+r,y+r,z+z_{d_1}^1+z_{d_2}^2),\)

<tbc>for some choice of \(d_1,d_2\in[1,r]\). We claim that critical path \(P_{d_1,d_2}^u\in\mathcal{P}\) is a \(u\rightsquigarrow v\) path in _G_. Notice that by construction, path \(P_{d_1,d_2}^u\) begins at node _u_ and ends at node \(v'\), where

\(v'=\left(2r,x+r,y+r,z+\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}f_{d_1}(i)+\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}f_{d_2}(i)\right)=(2r,x+r,y+r,z+z_{d_1}^1+z_{d_2}^2)=v.\)

We conclude that \(P_{d_1,d_2}^u\) is a \(u\rightsquigarrow v\) path in _G_, as claimed.

Finally, we verify that for every \(s\rightsquigarrow t\) path \(P_{d_1,d_2}^s\in\mathcal{P}\), there exists an \(s\rightsquigarrow t\) path in \(G\cup H\) of length two. Notice that by our construction of P, if \(P_{d_1,d_2}^s\) is an \(s\rightsquigarrow t\) path, then nodes _s_ and _t_ can be written as<tbc>

\(s=(0,x,y,z)\text{and}t=\left(2r,x+r,y+r,z+z_{d_1}^1+z_{d_2}^2\right).\)

<tbc>Then we can identify the following \(s\rightsquigarrow t\) path in \(G\cup H\) of length two:

\((0,x,y,z)\rightarrow(-1,x+r,y,z+z_{d_1}^1)\rightarrow\left(2r,x+r,y+r,z+z_{d_1}^1+z_{d_2}^2\right).\)

This completes the proof of Theorem C.3.
